title: ‘Forget AI treaty, go with shared standards’
full_text:
Foreign Minister Penny Wong has argued for shared standards among like-minded nations on AI rather than a binding international treaty, arguing the pace of change outstrips the deliberations of global institutions.
Speaking at a Q&A with the United States Study Centre in her first major public appearance since the US midterm elections, Senator Wong was quiet on the upheaval against the Trump administration but said Australia would try to “shape” America’s Indo-Pacific priorities.
Senator Wong’s push to sidestep global forums like the UN and instead push for matched legislative expectations on AI companies was a pragmatic step to match the quick pace of chance, she said.
“We don’t have the time to create a big treaty, so I think what we will see is more articulation of international laws and standards that may not be part of a treaty but that we seek to have adopted in various other countries,” she said.
“There is a desire around the world – amongst many countries – for there to be appropriate protections. We are engaged in that, but there’s a lot of work to do.”
Senator Wong said the Australian public supported the US alliance regardless of “the government of the day, whatever the issues”.
“They understand its relevance to our national security and our national interest and to stability in the region,” she said.
On Pacific relations, she argued American policy could be moulded by Australian priorities. It comes as Anthony Albanese travels to The Philippines to sign a joint defence agreement.
“We have a different understanding of – insight into and relationships with – the Pacific and also Southeast Asia, and we certainly bring that to the alliance,” Senator Wong said.
“Shaping how the US engages with those regions, or seeking to influence that, is very important from Australia’s perspective. It’s our near region, that’s where our stability and future prosperity lie.”
Her remarks on AI articulate the preferred method for delivering global safety standards she lobbied for during an address to the UN Security Council last year.
At the time, Senator Wong said the international community “must set the rules and establish the norms” for the emerging technology. “We must establish standards for the use of AI to demand it is safe, secure, responsible and ethical. To ensure AI transforms the tools of conflict and diplomacy for the better, the Security Council must lead by example – to strengthen international peace and security and ensure it is not undermined,” she said at the time.
On Friday, she used the pace of change in AI technologies to argue against a treaty-style regulation, saying it was “disrupting more quickly, more rapidly and more comprehensively than probably any previous technology”.
“We therefore have to work out how to deal with it, how we utilise it and engage with it in a way that enhances Australia’s sovereignty is central to Australian security and prosperity in the near future,” she said.
Anthony Albanese in September joined more than 20 other signatories in a statement to the Security Council saying the development of AI “could outpace our ability to manage emerging risks”, arguing the UN should pursue global guardrails.
The push for common standards matches Australia’s approach to social media regulation, where it has encouraged other countries to mirror Labor’s teen social media ban in the hopes of collectively wrangling multinational tech companies.
